title: The Spring Southwest Sold a Plane and Kept Its Timetable
conflicts: Bank balance: Southwest's anniversary site says $143 left in spring 1972, the Handbook of Texas says $148 in January 1971 (same anecdote, different dates), so none is given. Losses: Southwest and NPR imply $1.6 million by the sale, but the annual reports (via Wikipedia) give $3.8 million for 1971 and $1.6 million for all of 1972, so no loss figure is used. Gain on sale: $500,000 (Southwest) vs 'a small gain' (Wikipedia), attributed to the company. Reason for sale: cash (Southwest, NPR, Airways) vs a federal ruling against interstate charters (AvGeekery); story says only that losses went on. Competitors' gate time: an hour (Southwest) vs thirty minutes or more (Handbook of Texas); thirty used. Fourth plane arrived September (Southwest) or October 1971 (Wikipedia); 'that autumn' used.
notes: The slate named Kelleher and King, but the sale was Lamar Muse's decision and the turn is credited to Bill Franklin; the founder field names Muse and Franklin, with Kelleher and King as co-founders, and the story covers all four accurately. Arc changed from hard-responsibility to setback. Franklin's 'We can... And we will' is framed as the company's telling (NPR calls it legend). Southwest 50 page cited via the Wayback Machine. Quote stance: complicates.
